title: Justice at the Gate and a King Under the Law
summary: Moses continues the laws for Israel's life in the land: offerings must be unblemished, a proven idolater is to be executed only on the testimony of two or three witnesses, and hard cases go up to the priests and the judge at the central sanctuary. The chapter closes with the law of the king, which allows Israel a king but binds him under the same instruction as everyone else.
story: Israel is camped on the plains of Moab, east of the Jordan, and Moses is giving his last addresses before the people cross into Canaan without him. Chapters 12 to 26 form the central law code of Deuteronomy, and from 16:18 onward Moses turns to the offices that will govern the nation: judges, priests, the king, and (in chapter 18) the prophet. Chapter 17 sits in the middle of that section. It ties worship and justice together, since both answer to the same God, and it anticipates a day when Israel will want a king. That day arrives in 1 Samuel 8, and the rest of the Old Testament's history (Saul, David, Solomon, and the divided kingdoms) can be read as a long test of whether Israel's kings kept this chapter.
historical:
Deuteronomy presents itself as Moses' speeches in the land of Moab (1:1-5), given at the end of the wilderness years. Jewish and Christian tradition has taken Moses as its source, which would place it in the fifteenth or thirteenth century BC, depending on the date given to the exodus. Many modern scholars instead connect the book, in its present form, with the reform of King Josiah of Judah around 622 BC, when a book of the law was found in the temple (2 Kings 22-23), and see its emphasis on one central place of worship as reflecting that reform. Others argue that its covenant structure resembles second-millennium Hittite treaties, while another group points to seventh-century Assyrian loyalty oaths. The question is still debated, and readers on every side agree the book speaks to Israel on the edge of the land.

The law of the king is striking in the ancient world. Monarchy was the normal form of government across the Near East, and kings in Egypt and Mesopotamia were often presented as sons of the gods or as the source of law. Here the king is chosen by God, must be an Israelite, and receives no power to make law at all. The three things he is forbidden to multiply (horses, wives, and silver and gold) are exactly the things Solomon later gathered in great quantities, according to 1 Kings 10 and 11: horses imported from Egypt, hundreds of wives who turned his heart, and silver made common in Jerusalem. The historians of Kings seem to have written with this chapter in view.
cultural:
The town gate was Israel's courthouse. Elders sat there, business was witnessed there, and executions took place just outside it, which is why the offender is brought out to your gates in verse 5. Stoning was a communal act, and the rule that the witnesses throw the first stones made accusation costly: a man who lied under oath had to act on his lie with his own hands before the whole town. The requirement of two or three witnesses protected the accused from a single enemy's word.

Horses in this period were military technology, used for chariots rather than farming, and Egypt was a known source of them. A king who multiplied horses was building a standing chariot army and trusting it. Many wives usually meant political marriages with foreign royal houses, each bringing her own gods. Heaped-up treasure meant taxes and forced labor. The command that the king write out a copy of the law in the presence of the Levitical priests was unusual too: the ruler was to be a student of a text he did not write. The Greek translation of this verse, which rendered the phrase as a second law, gave the book its familiar English name, Deuteronomy.
literary: The chapter is law in the form of case law and address. The pattern of if a man or woman, then you must appears in verses 2-7, followed by a procedural law for difficult cases (verses 8-13) and a longer when you enter the land law for kingship (verses 14-20). Two refrains bind the sections together. One is the phrase to purge the evil from among you (verses 7 and 12), which recurs throughout Deuteronomy. The other is the image of not turning to the right or to the left, applied first to the people who receive the court's verdict (verse 11) and then to the king himself (verse 20). The same road that binds the ordinary Israelite binds the man on the throne.

outline.t: Idolatry proved by two or three witnesses
Difficult cases taken to the central court
The king God chooses and what he must not multiply
The king as a lifelong student of the law

doctrines.note: The law stands above every office in Israel, including the king's. Authority is real but derived: judges and priests give verdicts according to the instruction, and the king reads the same scroll as the people so that his heart will not be exalted above his countrymen.

Worship of other gods, including the sun, moon, and stars, is treated as a breach of covenant, the national equivalent of treason. The chapter also shows how easily power itself becomes an idol: horses, wives, and wealth are the king's temptations to trust something other than God.
God permits a human king but defines kingship on his own terms. The king is chosen by God, is a brother among brothers, and rules as the first servant of God's word rather than as its author.

words.note: Melek, king. The ordinary word for a ruler throughout the ancient Near East. Here it is carefully hedged: Israel may set a king over itself, but only the one the LORD chooses, and only under the instruction. The word sets up a tension that runs through the rest of the Old Testament between human kings and the kingship of God.

Torah, instruction or law. The word's range is wider than a legal code; it means teaching or direction. In verse 18 it refers to Moses' instruction as a written document, and the king is to read it all the days of his life. Deuteronomy uses the word for its own teaching, and later Judaism applied it to the whole Pentateuch.

Ba'ar, literally to burn, and so to consume or purge. Deuteronomy's refrain to purge the evil from among you uses it for the removal of serious wrongdoing from the covenant community. Paul echoes this refrain when he tells the Corinthians to remove an unrepentant man from their fellowship (1 Corinthians 5:13).

Ed, witness. The chapter's safeguard for justice rests on this word: no one dies on the testimony of a lone witness, and the witnesses must act first in carrying out the sentence. The principle is repeated in 19:15 and carried into the New Testament for church discipline and apostolic judgment.

christ: Israel's kings failed this chapter, most famously Solomon, and the prophets began to long for a king who would actually rule according to God's instruction. The New Testament presents Jesus as that king: a son of David who does not multiply horses but rides into Jerusalem on a donkey (Matthew 21:5), who owns nothing and gives his life for his people, and who does not turn aside from his Father's will to the right or to the left. The two-or-three-witnesses rule also runs into the New Testament directly. Jesus applies it to discipline among his followers (Matthew 18:16), Paul applies it to accusations in the church (2 Corinthians 13:1; 1 Timothy 5:19), and Hebrews recalls that the law of Moses executed on such testimony in order to show how much greater is the grace that is now refused (Hebrews 10:28-29). The link to Christ in the law of the king is a pattern and a longing rather than a prediction.

hard.q: Why does the law command the death penalty for worshiping other gods?
hard.a:
To a modern reader, executing someone for religious belief sounds like the definition of persecution, and the question deserves a straight answer. Deuteronomy frames Israel as a nation in covenant with God, with the LORD as its king, so worship of other gods was treated as treason against the nation's sovereign and a threat to the whole community's life in the land. The law also restrains the penalty: a thorough investigation is required, two or three witnesses are needed, and the witnesses bear the first responsibility.

Christians have read these laws in different ways. Most traditions hold that the civil penalties belonged to Israel as a political nation under the old covenant and do not transfer to the church, which has no sword; the New Testament's parallel is exclusion from fellowship, not execution (1 Corinthians 5). A smaller group, sometimes called theonomists, argues that the civil laws still offer a model for modern states. Jewish tradition developed its own safeguards, and the rabbis made capital sentences extremely difficult to carry out. On any reading, the chapter treats idolatry as deadly serious and justice as something that must never rest on rumor.

questions: The king was told to read God's instruction all his life so that his heart would not be exalted above his countrymen. What habits keep people with authority humble?
Horses, wives, and wealth were the king's particular temptations. What does a leader in your world tend to multiply in order to feel secure?
The rule of two or three witnesses protected the accused from rumor. How careful are you with accusations you hear about others?
